'''''Guilandina bonduc''''', commonly known as '''nicker nut''' amongst other names, is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the bean family [[Fabaceae]] that has a mostly [[pantropical]] distribution. It is a scrambling, thorny shrub or vine that is mostly found close to coastlines, and was first described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]].

==Description==
''Guilandina bonduc'' grows as a scrambling shrub or climber, up to {{convert|8|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}} long. The stems are irregularly covered with curved prickles. The leaves are large and bi-pinnate, up to {{convert|40|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long with scattered prickles on the rachises and blades. There are four to eleven pairs of pinnae, {{convert|5|to|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long with five to ten pairs of pinnules. The pinnules are {{convert|15|to|40|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long, elliptic, oblong or ovate with acute tips and entire margins.<ref name=Hawaii>{{cite web |url=http://www.nativeplants.hawaii.edu/plant/view/Caesalpinia_bonduc |title=''Guilandina bonduc'' |work=Native Plants: Hawaii |publisher= |access-date=11 September 2020 }}</ref><ref name="RPoT">{{Cite book |last=Whistler |first=Art |url=https://www.cepf.net/sites/default/files/sg51070-final-report.pdf |title=The Rare Plants of Tonga |publisher=Tonga Trust Ltd |year=2011 |pages=89–90}}</ref>

The inflorescence is an axillary raceme, often branched, covered with short hairs and up to {{convert|15|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long. The jointed pedicels are up to {{convert|6|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long. The sepals are shorter than the petals which are around {{convert|10|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long; the petals are yellow, sometimes with a spot of orange near the base of the keel. The unisexual flowers are followed by large, flattish, spiny green pods which later turn brown, some {{convert|9|by|4|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}, containing one or usually two, glossy, rounded, grey seeds.<ref name="Hawaii"/><ref name="RPoT"/>

Its {{convert|2|cm|in|1|abbr=on|adj=on}} grey seeds are buoyant and durable enough to be dispersed by ocean currents.<ref name="Nelson">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wzmo7cHvhZkC |first=Gil |last=Nelson |title=The Shrubs and Woody Vines of Florida: a Reference and Field Guide |publisher=Pineapple Press Inc |isbn=978-1-56164-110-9 |year=1996 |pages=177–178}}</ref><ref name="Cody">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aw_2IHOD8fQC |first=Martin L. |last=Cody |title=Plants on Islands: Diversity and Dynamics on a Continental Archipelago |publisher=University of California Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-520-24729-1 |page=161}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Guilandina bonduc'' occurs in tropical and subtropical regions of the world, and is present on all continents except Antarctica.{{R|POWO}} It typically grows near the coast, in scrub, on sand dunes and on the upper shore.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.mozambiqueflora.com/speciesdata/species.php?species_id=180050 |title=''Guilandina bonduc'' L. |publisher=Flora of Mozambique |access-date=12 September 2020 }}</ref> It also occurs inland, in lowland secondary forest and disturbed areas near villages; this may be the result of the seed being accidentally dropped after being transported for medical purposes or for use as counters in board games. The seeds are buoyant and retain their viability in both fresh and sea water, enabling them to disperse to new coastal locations.<ref name=Fern>{{cite web |url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Guilandina+bonduc&redir=Caesalpinia+bonduc |title=''Guilandina bonduc'' |author=Fern, Ken|publisher=Useful tropical plants |access-date=12 September 2020 }}</ref> When washed up on the shore, they are sometimes known as sea pearls.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.seabean.com/guide/Caesalpinia_bonduc/index.htm |title=Gray Nickarbean or Sea Pearl |publisher=A Sea-Bean Guide |access-date=12 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081225171216/http://www.seabean.com/guide/Caesalpinia_bonduc/index.htm |archive-date=25 December 2008 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
This plant was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book ''Species plantarum'', published in 1753.{{R|POWO|LINNAEUS}} For a time some authorities accepted the name ''Caesalpinia bonduc'' which was proposed by Scottish botanist [[William Roxburgh]] in 1824, but that has been synonymised with ''G. bonduc''.{{R|PLANTNET|POWO2}}

==Common names==
Due to its wide distribution in many countries and cultures, this plant has numerous common names. These include gray nicker,{{R|NPSING}} grey nicker, grey nickerbean, yellow nickers, nicker nut, wait-a-while,{{R|RFK}} bonduc and nivi-nivi,{{R|GRIN}} along with numerous others.{{R|PROTA4U}}

==Uses==
Nodules on the plant's roots contain [[symbiosis|symbiotic]] bacteria that [[nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]]. This is used as a nutrient by the vine and also benefits other plants growing in close proximity.<ref name=Fern/> It is a popular local ornamental plant in Malaysia.<ref name="MGfM">{{cite book|author1=Lee Shin Shin |author2=Aziah Muhamad |author3=Joanne Tong |title=Mangrove Guidebook for Malaysia |year=2015 |location=Petaling Jaya, Selangor, Malaysia |publisher=Wetlands International, Malaysia |page=85 |isbn=978-983-42276-6-1}}</ref>

This plant has been used in traditional medicine. The seeds have tonic and antipyretic properties and the bark and leaves have been used likewise. The root can be pounded to remedy caterpillar stings, it can be boiled and its broth drank to regulate [[menstruation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Burkill |first=Isaac Henry |author2=Mohamad Haniff |date=April 1930 |title=Malay Village Medicine: prescriptions collected by I.H. Burkill and Mohamad Haniff |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/43666335#page/212/mode/1up |journal=The Gardens' Bulletin; Straits Settlements |volume=6 |issue=3 (part 2) |pages=165–273 }}</ref>{{rp|196}} An oil extracted from the seeds has been used in cosmetics and for treating discharges from the ear.<ref name=India>{{cite web |url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Fever%20Nut.html |title=Fever nut |publisher=Flowers of India |access-date=12 September 2020 }}</ref>

[[Tonga|Tongans]] make the hard seeds (''talatala 'amoa'') into [[Lei (garland)|leis]] or play with them like marbles; its spiky leaves and stems are used in [[fruit bat]] snares.<ref name="RPoT" />
